title: Deep in one: Isaiah
subtitle: Twelve sessions through the grandest of the prophets: the holy God, Immanuel, the nations, comfort for exiles, the suffering servant and new heavens and a new earth.
intro: This track reads Isaiah in twelve sittings. It is the longest of the prophetic books, sixty-six chapters, mostly poetry, and the New Testament quotes it more than almost any other. It speaks into three moments: Jerusalem under the threat of Assyria, the exiles in Babylon a century and a half later, and a people back in the land but still waiting. The track takes those settings in turn, and names the questions faithful readers still argue over without settling them for you.

Each session opens a chapter of the Study Bible with its notes in plain words, and comes back to one question, one thing to do and one verse. Read the chapters the session names before you begin it, aloud if you can, because Isaiah was spoken before it was written. Watch for the words the Gospels borrow: Immanuel, a voice in the wilderness, a light for the nations, a servant pierced for our transgressions. By the end you should be able to explain to a friend why Christians call Isaiah the fifth gospel, and why Jewish readers hear it differently. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: Isaiah. The group meets twelve times and reads a part of the book each time, from the prophet's call in the temple to the new heavens and new earth. It suits people who already believe and people who are only curious, because Isaiah asks what everyone under a powerful empire asks: whom to trust, whether God has forgotten his people, and whether suffering can ever be for someone else's good.

Each person reads the chapters and the session before the group meets. The meeting reads the heart of the passage aloud and talks it over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for twelve meetings, and keep the end time you promised. Isaiah is long and the track chooses its chapters, so encourage people to read around them when they can, and don't try to cover everything in the room. A leader doesn't need to be a scholar. A leader needs to have read the chapters and their notes, and to be willing to admit not knowing.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit in a circle round a table if you can, with the text open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. Isaiah is poetry meant to be heard, so ask a good reader to read the central passage aloud at each meeting, slowly, and let people take turns. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own lives stays in the room, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Fifteen minutes: one person reads the central passage aloud while the others follow.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is in the text.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words.
Five minutes: name the next passage and the page its session opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Isaiah raises questions scholars and churches have argued over for a long time: who wrote the book and when, whether the sign of Immanuel spoke first of a child in Ahaz's day, who the servant is, and how its last verse of judgment should be read. When the group reaches one, read the note on it together before anyone answers. Give each reading its strongest form, in words its own holders would sign, and don't settle for the group what the church has not settled. If no one knows, write the question down and bring it back the next week.

Some of these questions divide Christians and Jews, and the servant song of chapter 53 most of all. State the Jewish reading fairly and with respect. The track never gives anyone a warrant for contempt toward the Jewish people, and neither should the group. Treating a question as disloyalty ends the conversation, and Isaiah himself argued with God about how long.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Isaiah speaks to people who have lost their homes, their city and their sense that God remembers them. Someone in the group may be living through something close to that: grief, illness, exile from a country or a family, or a long wait for an answer. When that happens, stop the discussion and listen. Thank the person for saying it, don't explain their suffering for them, and don't hurry them back to the passage. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

The servant who suffers for others is never a reason for someone to stay where they are being harmed, and the promise of healing is never a judgment on the faith of the sick. If someone says that a partner, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, fear or guilt that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: Isaiah's world and the book's three settings
teaching: Isaiah son of Amoz preached in Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, through the reigns of four kings of Judah (Isaiah 1:1), while Assyria swallowed the small nations around him. His call came at the end of King Uzziah's reign (Isaiah 6:1), usually placed about 740 BC. The book speaks into three settings. Chapters 1 to 39 belong to Isaiah's own Jerusalem under the shadow of Assyria. Chapters 40 to 55 speak to exiles in Babylon a century and a half later, and name the Persian king Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1). Chapters 56 to 66 speak to a people back in the land but still waiting.

Who wrote it all is a real question, and faithful readers answer it differently. The traditional view, held for most of the church's history and defended by scholars such as J. Alec Motyer and John Oswalt, is that Isaiah gave the whole book, and that the later chapters are true prophecy given in advance. From the late eighteenth century many scholars have argued that chapters 40 to 66 come from later prophets, and since Bernhard Duhm in 1892 many speak of First, Second and Third Isaiah. Others hold that Isaiah's disciples carried his words on. This track leaves the question open. On every view the church receives the book as God's word, and reads it whole.

open.label: Isaiah's introduction in the Study Bible
open.why: Isaiah's world, Assyria, Babylon and Cyrus, how the book is built, and each view of its authorship set out as its holders state it.

also.label: Isaiah: the whole book
also.why: The whole book in a few short pictures, its three movements and its great promises, before you read it part by part.

also.label: How to read the prophets
also.why: What a prophet was, how prophetic poetry works, and how to read promises that speak to more than one moment.

also.label: The Bible's timeline
also.why: Where Isaiah's kings, the fall of Samaria, the exile and the return to Jerusalem sit in the whole story of the Bible.

sessions.question: Isaiah speaks into three different moments in his people's life. Which of them, threat, exile or waiting, feels most like the moment you are in?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 1, 40 and 65 in one sitting, one from each part of the book. Write down one thing that is the same in all three, and one thing that has changed.

verse.text: The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever.

group.open: What do you already know, or think you know, about Isaiah?
discuss: Why might it help to know which of the three settings a chapter speaks to before you read it?
Christians hold different views on who wrote Isaiah. What is at stake in the question, and what is not?
Isaiah's first readers lived under an empire they could not control. Where do people feel that way now?
group.pray: Pray for the group as you begin, that the God who spoke through Isaiah would give each of you ears to hear him across the centuries.

sessions.title: The vineyard and the call
teaching: Chapter 5 opens as a love song about a vineyard and turns into a verdict. The owner did everything for his vines, and they gave him wild grapes. Then the prophet names the vineyard: “He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress” (Isaiah 5:7). In Hebrew the words rhyme, justice with bloodshed and righteousness with a cry, the way a counterfeit resembles the real thing. Six woes follow, on those who add house to house, who call evil good, who are heroes at drinking wine. Judah's sin is not exotic. It is greed, spin and comfort.

Then, at the end of Uzziah's reign, Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne and hears the seraphim: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory” (Isaiah 6:3). His first word is not praise but ruin, because he is a man of unclean lips among a people of unclean lips. A coal touches his mouth, his guilt is taken away, and only then is he sent. The message he is given is hard, a word that will harden those who refuse it, and Jesus quoted it of his own hearers (Mark 4:12). John says that “Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus’ glory” (John 12:41).

open.label: Isaiah 6, passage by passage
open.why: The throne, the seraphim, the coal and the hard commission, explained in plain words, with how the New Testament takes up the vision.

also.label: Holiness
also.why: What Scripture means when it calls God holy, three times over, and what his holiness does to the people who see it.

also.label: What justice meant
also.why: What the prophets meant by justice and righteousness in their own world, the very words the vineyard song turns on.

sessions.question: Isaiah saw God's holiness and at once saw his own uncleanness. Why do you think the two came together?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 5:1-7 aloud, then Isaiah 6. Write down what Isaiah sees, what he says, what is done for him, and what he is sent to do, in that order.

verse.text: Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying: “Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?” And I said: “Here am I. Send me!”

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you been in the presence of something so great that it made you feel small?
discuss: The vineyard song turns from a love song into a verdict. What does it show about how God sees injustice?
Isaiah is cleansed before he is sent. Why does that order matter for anyone who serves God?
Isaiah's message would harden many who heard it. How do you understand a call to speak to people who may not listen?
group.pray: Confess quietly the ways the group's lives have given wild grapes, give thanks for the coal that takes guilt away, and ask to be sent.

sessions.title: Immanuel, in Ahaz's day and in Matthew's
teaching: Around 735 BC the kings of Aram and Israel march on Jerusalem to force Judah into their alliance against Assyria, and the hearts of King Ahaz and his people “trembled like trees in the forest shaken by the wind” (Isaiah 7:2). Isaiah meets the king with a word: “If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all” (Isaiah 7:9). Ahaz is offered a sign and refuses, because he has already decided to buy Assyria's help. So a sign is given anyway: a child called Immanuel, God with us. Before the boy knows good from evil, the two kings Ahaz dreads will be gone, and by 732 BC they were.

So who is the child? The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age, and many Jewish and Christian scholars read the sign first as a child born in Ahaz's day. Matthew reads it of Jesus, quoting the Greek translation made by Jewish scholars before Christianity, which has virgin (Matthew 1:23). Christians hold that the verse is direct prophecy, or that it had a near fulfilment and a fuller one, or that Matthew sees in Jesus the completion of a pattern. The next chapters reach past any ordinary child: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given” (Isaiah 9:6), and among his names is Mighty God.

open.label: Isaiah 7, passage by passage
open.why: Ahaz's panic, Isaiah's word and the sign of Immanuel, explained in plain words, with each reading of the sign set out fairly.

also.label: Messianic expectation
also.why: What Jews of Jesus' day hoped for in a Messiah, and which promises of Isaiah they read with that hope.

also.label: The Messiah
also.why: The promise of an anointed king traced through the Old Testament, and how the New Testament finds it in Jesus.

sessions.question: Ahaz refused a sign because he had already chosen his own way out. Where are you tempted to ask God for help after you have already decided?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 7:1-17, then 9:1-7, then Matthew 1:18-25. Write down what the sign meant for Ahaz, and what Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus.

verse.text: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.

group.open: When have you been badly shaken by something that passed far more quickly than you expected?
discuss: Isaiah tells Ahaz that faith is the only firm ground. Why was trusting Assyria easier for Ahaz than trusting God?
Faithful Christians read Isaiah 7:14 in more than one way. What does each reading take seriously in the text?
The child of chapter 9 is called Mighty God and Prince of Peace. What does it mean that Immanuel is God with us, and not only a sign that God is for us?
group.pray: Pray for anyone in the group who is shaken by events they cannot control, and give thanks for Immanuel, God with us.

sessions.title: The branch and the peaceable kingdom
teaching: By chapter 10 the house of David looks like a forest cut down. Then: “a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:1). Jesse was David's father, so the promise reaches back past the failed kings to the root of the family. The Spirit of the LORD rests on this branch, with wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, and he rules as no king of Judah did: “with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth” (Isaiah 11:4). The test of his reign is how the poor fare under it.

Then the picture widens: the wolf with the lamb, the leopard with the goat, a child playing over a snake's den, because “the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water” (Isaiah 11:9). Some read this as a promise that creation itself will be renewed, others as a poet's picture of peace among peoples, and many hold both. The Gospels show the Spirit coming to rest on Jesus at his baptism, and Paul quotes this chapter's root of Jesse as a hope for the nations (Romans 15:12). The peace Isaiah sees is more than a pause in trouble. It is a world set right.

open.label: Isaiah 11, passage by passage
open.why: The shoot from Jesse's stump, the Spirit on him, his justice for the poor and the peaceable kingdom, explained in plain words.

also.label: The King
also.why: Short pictures of the promised king through the Bible, from David's line to the one Isaiah saw rising from a stump.

also.label: Justice and the poor
also.why: What Scripture and the church's long practice say about the poor, for readers who take the branch's test as their own.

sessions.question: Isaiah's king is judged by how the poor fare under his reign. What would change if that were the test you used for yourself?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 11 slowly. Underline everything the Spirit gives the branch, and circle everything that changes because of his reign.

verse.text: They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water.

group.open: If you could see one thing in the world set right in your lifetime, what would it be?
discuss: Why does the promise reach back to Jesse rather than to David or to the kings after him?
Christians read the wolf and the lamb as renewed creation, as a picture of peace among peoples, or both. What is gained by each reading?
The branch judges the poor with righteousness. Who are the poor and lowly in your own town, and how are they treated?
group.pray: Pray for the poor and lowly where you live, by name where you can, and ask for the Spirit who rested on the branch to rest on the church.

sessions.title: The nations under judgment
teaching: Chapters 13 to 23 are a run of oracles, each called a burden, against the nations around Judah: Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Cush, Egypt, Edom, Arabia and Tyre. Isaiah's hearers were tempted to fear these powers or to lean on them. The prophet tells them that each stands under the judgment of the same God, and that pride brings every one of them down. The taunt over the king of Babylon, “How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn” (Isaiah 14:12), was later read by many Christians as the fall of Satan, though the chapter itself names a human king.

Then, in the middle of the burden against Egypt, comes one of the most startling promises in the Old Testament. Egypt, the old house of slavery, and Assyria, the empire that crushed Israel, will worship beside Israel, and the LORD will say, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance” (Isaiah 19:25). Judgment on the nations isn't the end of God's purpose for them. Isaiah sees enemies made into family. It is the hope Paul preached as Gentiles came into the church, and it ought to unsettle every reader who is sure which nations God is against.

open.label: Isaiah 19, passage by passage
open.why: The burden against Egypt and the promise that Egypt and Assyria will worship beside Israel, explained in plain words.

also.label: The Bible atlas
also.why: Find the nations of Isaiah 13 to 23 on the map, from Babylon in the east to Tyre on the coast and Cush in the south.

also.label: The empires of the Bible
also.why: Assyria, Babylon, Persia and the rest: who ruled when, and how each empire shaped the lives of Isaiah's hearers.

also.label: All nations
also.why: Short pictures of God's purpose for every nation, from the promise to Abraham to the crowd from every tongue in Revelation.

sessions.question: Isaiah names Egypt and Assyria as God's people. Which nation or group would it most unsettle you to hear God call his own?
sessions.do: Find the nations of Isaiah 13 to 23 on the Bible atlas. Then read Isaiah 19:16-25 and write down what God does to Egypt, and what he does for it.

verse.text: The LORD of Hosts will bless them, saying, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.”

care: If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Which country or people did you grow up thinking of as the enemy?
discuss: Why do you think Isaiah spends eleven chapters on the nations around Judah?
Pride is what brings each nation down. Where do you see the same pride in powerful nations now, including your own?
What would it take for the church to believe that God's purpose for its enemies includes blessing?
group.pray: Pray for the nations in the news this week, including those your own country counts as enemies, and for the church in each of them.

sessions.title: The little apocalypse
teaching: After the nations one by one, chapters 24 to 27 widen to the whole earth. They are often called the Isaiah apocalypse, and when they were written is debated, from Isaiah's own day to the Persian period. The earth is laid waste because its people have “broken the everlasting covenant” (Isaiah 24:5), and a city of chaos falls. Then the scene turns to a mountain and a feast: “the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples” (Isaiah 25:6), and “He will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8). The God who judges the whole earth means to feed it.

Chapter 26 adds a line that some scholars read as one of the Old Testament's clearest hopes of resurrection: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19). Others read it as a picture of the nation raised from exile, like Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, and many see both. Paul quotes Isaiah 25:8 when he writes of the resurrection of the body (1 Corinthians 15:54), and the last pages of the Bible take up its promise that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4). The shroud over all peoples is death itself, and God will take it away.

open.label: Isaiah 25, passage by passage
open.why: The banquet on the mountain and the promise that death will be swallowed up, explained in plain words, with care for readers who grieve.

also.label: How to read apocalyptic
also.why: How visions of the end of the world work, their pictures and numbers, and how to read them without forcing them into a timetable.

also.label: The resurrection
also.why: The hope of the body raised, traced from Isaiah and Daniel to the empty tomb and Paul's chapter on the resurrection.

also.label: The life to come
also.why: Short pictures of what the Bible says lies ahead, the resurrection and the new creation Isaiah glimpsed on the mountain.

sessions.question: Isaiah pictures death as a shroud over all peoples that God will swallow. What would it change to believe that about someone you have lost?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 25:6-9 and Revelation 21:1-5 side by side. Write down every word or picture the two passages share.

verse.text: He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face and remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth. For the LORD has spoken.

care: Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is the best feast or celebration meal you have ever been part of, and what made it so?
discuss: Why do you think Isaiah pictures the end not only as judgment but as a banquet for all peoples?
Scholars read Isaiah 26:19 as resurrection, as national restoration, or both. What would each reading have meant to people in exile?
If death is a shroud God will swallow, how should Christians grieve, and how should they not?
group.pray: Pray for anyone in the group who is grieving, without hurrying them, and give thanks for the promise that God will wipe away the tears from every face.

sessions.title: Hezekiah and the Assyrian siege
teaching: Chapters 36 to 39 change from poetry to story, and tell the same events as 2 Kings 18 to 20. In 701 BC Sennacherib of Assyria has taken the fortified towns of Judah, and he sends his field commander to the walls of Jerusalem with a speech that still sounds modern: “What is the basis of this confidence of yours?” (Isaiah 36:4). Egypt can't save you, he says, and neither can your God. Sennacherib's own annals boast that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage, and they don't claim the city fell. Hezekiah takes the threatening letter into the temple, spreads it before the LORD, and prays.

He asks for rescue “so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God” (Isaiah 37:20), and the city is spared. Then Hezekiah falls ill, prays again, and is given fifteen more years. But the section ends badly. Envoys come from Babylon, and Hezekiah shows them everything he owns. Isaiah tells him it will all be carried off to Babylon, and the king's private thought is chilling: “At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime” (Isaiah 39:8). The next chapter begins with comfort for exiles in Babylon. The story of a faithful king ends by pointing past him.

open.label: Isaiah 37, passage by passage
open.why: Hezekiah's prayer over the letter, Isaiah's answer and the city spared, explained in plain words, with what Assyria's own records say.

also.label: The kings of Israel and Judah
also.why: Every king of the divided kingdom in order, with the ways their dates are counted, so Ahaz and Hezekiah have a place.

also.label: The prophets and the exile
also.why: Where Isaiah stands in the Bible's story, between the kings who failed and the exile he warned of.

sessions.question: Hezekiah spread the threatening letter before God. What letter, message or worry would you spread before him this week?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 36 and 37. Then write what troubles you most on a sheet of paper, and lay it open in front of you as you pray, as Hezekiah did.

verse.text: O LORD of Hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth.

care: It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When has someone tried to talk you out of your hope? What did they say?
discuss: The Assyrian commander asks what the basis of Judah's confidence is. It is a real question. How would you answer it?
Hezekiah prays that the nations would know God, not only that Jerusalem would be safe. What does that teach us about praying in a crisis?
Hezekiah is content that trouble will come after his lifetime. Where are we tempted to the same comfort, and who pays for it?
group.pray: Lay the group's real worries before God together, naming them plainly, and pray for those who will live with the choices made in your lifetime.

sessions.title: Comfort, comfort my people
teaching: Between chapters 39 and 40 the horizon moves on a century and a half. Jerusalem has fallen and the people are in Babylon, and the first words to them are tender: “Comfort, comfort My people” (Isaiah 40:1). A voice calls for a highway in the desert, a new exodus, with God leading his people home as he once led them out of Egypt. All four Gospels take up that voice for John the Baptist, and Mark opens with it: “Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him” (Mark 1:3).

Then the chapter sets two things side by side. People are grass, and “the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). The idols have to be fastened down so they won't topple, while the LORD calls every star by name. The exiles thought their God had lost to Babylon's gods, or forgotten them. Isaiah's answer is that he is the Creator of the ends of the earth, who doesn't grow tired, and who gives his strength to the weary who wait for him. Waiting here is not idleness. It is trusting God's timing when his people can't see it.

open.label: Isaiah 40, passage by passage
open.why: The comfort, the voice in the wilderness, the grass and the word, the idols and the stars, explained in plain words.

also.label: Exile and home
also.why: Short pictures of the exile to Babylon and the road home, the world into which Isaiah 40 first spoke comfort.

also.label: Isaiah 41:10 in context
also.why: A much-loved verse from the next chapter read in its setting among the exiles, and what it does and does not promise.

also.label: How to wait on God
also.why: Plain steps for the kind of waiting Isaiah means, trust kept up through a long delay rather than idle hoping.

sessions.question: The exiles believed God had forgotten them. Where do you need to hear the first words of Isaiah 40 spoken to you?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 40 aloud, slowly. Then read Mark 1:1-8 and write down why Mark might have chosen to open his Gospel with this chapter.

verse.text: But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint.

group.open: When has a kind word come to you at exactly the moment you needed it?
discuss: Why do you think the second half of Isaiah begins with comfort rather than with a rebuke?
Isaiah pictures a highway in the desert, a new exodus. What does it mean to say Jesus leads a new exodus?
What is the difference between waiting on God and simply waiting?
group.pray: Speak comfort to one another in prayer, naming the weary in the group and beyond it, and ask for strength to wait on the LORD.

sessions.title: The servant songs
teaching: From chapter 42 a figure appears whom God calls “My Servant” (Isaiah 42:1). He brings justice to the nations quietly: “A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish” (Isaiah 42:3). Who is he? Isaiah often names Israel as God's servant, and in one song God says, “You are My Servant, Israel” (Isaiah 49:3). Yet two verses later the servant's task is to bring Israel back to God. Jewish readers have long taken the servant to be Israel. Christians read him as the one who does what Israel was called to do, for Israel and for the nations.

The servant's calling is wider than anyone expected: “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). And it costs him. In the third song he says, “I offered My back to those who struck Me” (Isaiah 50:6), and he doesn't turn away. Matthew applies the first song to Jesus (Matthew 12:18), Simeon sings of a light for the Gentiles over the infant Jesus (Luke 2:32), and Paul and Barnabas take Isaiah 49:6 as their own commission (Acts 13:47).

open.label: Isaiah 42, passage by passage
open.why: The first servant song and the new song that follows it, explained in plain words, with the readings of who the servant is.

also.label: Isaiah 49, passage by passage
also.why: The second servant song, called from the womb and made a light for the nations, with Zion's fear that God has forgotten her.

also.label: Mission
also.why: God's purpose to bring his salvation to the ends of the earth, from the servant's calling to the church's.

sessions.question: The servant will not break a bruised reed. Who around you is bruised or barely burning, and how would the servant treat them?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 42:1-9, 49:1-7 and 50:4-9. For each song, write down who speaks, who the servant is said to be, and what the servant does.

verse.text: A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice.

care: If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who in your life has been gentle with you when you were at your weakest?
discuss: Jewish readers see the servant as Israel, Christians as one who fulfils Israel's calling. What in the songs supports each reading?
The servant brings justice without shouting. What does that say about how Christians should seek justice now?
The servant's calling is to be a light for the nations. How is that calling passed on to the church?
group.pray: Pray for the bruised and the barely burning in your lives, and ask that the church would be as gentle and as faithful as the servant.

sessions.title: The suffering servant
teaching: The fourth song begins with the servant lifted up and ends with him exalted, and between those lines is a passage the New Testament returns to again and again to explain the cross. The speakers say we: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3), and they confess they misjudged him. Then the turn: “But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). He suffers for their wrongs, not his own, and he doesn't open his mouth.

An Ethiopian official reading this aloud in his chariot asked Philip, “who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” (Acts 8:34), and it is still the first question. Rashi and most Jewish interpreters since have read the servant as Israel, humiliated among the nations, whose suffering the kings at last understand. Christians answer that this servant suffers without sin and for others, and Philip, starting from this Scripture, told the man the good news about Jesus. Here Jews and Christians most sharply part, and the song gives no one a warrant for contempt.

open.label: Study Isaiah 53, step by step
open.why: The guided study walks you through the suffering servant in seven steps, from reading the song aloud to praying it.

also.label: The atonement
also.why: What Christians mean by saying Christ died for sins, the ways the church has explained it, and the objections taken seriously.

also.label: Why Jesus died
also.why: Short pictures of the meaning of the cross, drawing on the servant who was pierced for our transgressions.

also.label: Christ in the Bible's story
also.why: Where Jesus' life, death and resurrection sit in the whole story, and how the Gospels read the Old Testament toward him.

sessions.question: The speakers in Isaiah 53 confess that they misjudged the servant. What would it mean for you to say we in that song?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12 aloud. Then read Acts 8:26-39, and write down how you would answer the Ethiopian's question if a friend asked it.

verse.text: But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.

care: It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you misjudged someone and later learned what they had carried for you?
discuss: Jewish readers see Israel in this song, Christians see Jesus. How can we state the other reading fairly, and why does it matter that we do?
Isaiah says the servant was crushed for our iniquities. What do Christians mean by saying Jesus died in our place, and which objections must they take seriously?
How should this song shape the way Christians speak about the Jewish people and to them?
group.pray: Give thanks for the servant who bore the sin of many, and pray for Jewish neighbours and friends with love and honour.

sessions.title: Come to the waters
teaching: After the servant's suffering comes an invitation that sounds like a street seller's cry: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat” (Isaiah 55:1). The cost has been paid elsewhere. What is asked is that people stop spending on bread that doesn't satisfy, and come. The invitation goes to the wicked as well, who are told to return to the LORD, “for He will freely pardon” (Isaiah 55:7). On the last day of a feast in Jerusalem Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink” (John 7:37).

The well-known line “My thoughts are not your thoughts” (Isaiah 55:8) is often quoted to mean that God is beyond understanding. In context it is about mercy. God's thoughts are higher because he pardons where people would not. Then rain and snow come down and don't go back without watering the earth, and so it is with his word: it “will not return to Me empty” (Isaiah 55:11). The chapter ends with cypress growing where thorns were and a people going out in joy, the whole creation joining the new exodus.

open.label: Isaiah 55, passage by passage
open.why: The invitation to the thirsty, the higher thoughts of mercy and the word that does not return empty, explained in plain words.

also.label: Money and the heart
also.why: What Scripture says about spending on what does not satisfy, and how money shapes what the heart loves.

also.label: Salvation
also.why: What the Bible means by being saved, a gift received without price, traced from Isaiah's invitation to the gospel.

sessions.question: What have you been spending your money and effort on that is not bread, and what would it mean to come to the waters instead?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 55 slowly, twice. The second time, mark every command, come, listen, seek, return, and the promise that goes with each.

verse.text: Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost!

group.open: What is the best free gift you have ever been given?
discuss: Why do people find it so hard to accept something they cannot pay for?
How does reading God's higher thoughts as being about mercy change the way the verse is often used?
God's word does not return empty. Where have you seen it do its work slowly, like rain?
group.pray: Pray for the thirsty you know, by name, and give thanks for a God who freely pardons.

sessions.title: New heavens and a new earth
teaching: Isaiah ends with creation made new: “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). The picture is ordinary and physical. People build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit, and children are not born for trouble. Weeping is heard no more in Jerusalem, and the wolf and the lamb feed together, as in chapter 11. Revelation takes up these chapters for its last vision: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21:1). The hope of the Bible is the world healed, not a way out of it.

But Isaiah does not close softly. The last verse speaks of those who rebelled, whose “worm will never die” (Isaiah 66:24), and Jesus used the same words in warning (Mark 9:48). Christians differ over what that judgment finally means, and the book doesn't ask you to settle it here. What it asks is the posture of chapter 66: God looks to the one “who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word” (Isaiah 66:2). The next track in this program is the Gospel of Mark, which opens with Isaiah's voice in the wilderness. Read it as the beginning of what Isaiah saw from far off.

open.label: Isaiah 65, passage by passage
open.why: The new heavens and new earth, the houses and vineyards, the wolf and the lamb, explained in plain words with care for readers who grieve.

also.label: The new creation
also.why: The Bible's hope for a world made new, from Isaiah's last chapters to the city coming down in Revelation.

also.label: The new creation in the Bible's story
also.why: The last act of the Bible's story, where everything Isaiah longed for comes home.

also.label: Deep in one: the Gospel of Mark
also.why: The next track in this program reads Mark a chapter at a time, beginning with the voice Isaiah heard in the wilderness.

sessions.question: Isaiah ends with both a new creation and a warning. Why do you think the book refuses to leave out either one?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 65:17-25 and Revelation 21:1-5. Then go back to Isaiah 1 and write down which of its griefs the last chapters answer, and which are still waiting.

verse.text: For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.

care: Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Which of these twelve sessions will stay with you longest, and why?
discuss: Isaiah's new creation has houses, vineyards and children. What does that ordinary picture say about what God means to save?
Why might Isaiah end with the warning of 66:24 rather than with the vision of chapter 65?
Jesus read Isaiah as being about himself. Having read the book, where do you most see him in it?
group.pray: Give thanks by name for each person in the group, and ask for humble and contrite hearts that tremble at God's word as you go on to read Mark.
